analysis.one_liner: Creates a tribally co-managed Grand Canyon national monument and withdraws the land from new mining claims.
analysis.headline: The bill to make 1,069,970 acres around the Grand Canyon a tribal co-stewarded national monument was referred to committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have turned about 1,069,970 acres of federal land around the Grand Canyon into a national monument run jointly by the Interior and Agriculture Departments, with a commission of 12 Arizona-area tribes advising management. It would have barred new mining claims and mineral leasing on that land while leaving existing mining rights, grazing, water rights, hunting, fishing, and recreational access untouched. It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: The 12 Associated Tribes — including the Havasupai, Hopi, Hualapai, Navajo Nation, and Zuni — would gain a formal Tribal commission, co-stewardship opportunities, self-determination contracts, and protected access to sacred sites. Hunters, anglers, hikers, campers, and mountain bikers would keep their existing access, which the bill's findings call the primary driver of sustainable economic development in nearby communities. The public would gain protection for the Grand Canyon watershed, whose groundwater feeds the Colorado River, a drinking water source for millions of Americans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Grand Canyon tribes and outdoor recreationists

how_it_helps.text: Would establish a roughly 1,069,970-acre Baaj Nwaavjo I'tah Kukveni Grand Canyon National Monument and withdraw the land from new mining claims and from mineral and geothermal leasing, subject to valid existing rights — blocking new uranium and other mining development near the canyon.

Would give the 12 Associated Tribes a formal seat in management: a Tribal commission whose guidance the Secretaries must consider, co-stewardship and cooperative agreements, self-determination contracts, protected access to sacred sites, and the ability to temporarily close small areas for cultural and religious activities.

Would preserve the uses people already rely on: hunting and fishing under state law, existing livestock grazing, water rights and interstate compacts, utility and road corridors, motorized access for hunting and emergencies, and general public access.

analysis.who_pays: Mining companies would lose the ability to stake new claims or obtain mineral and geothermal leases on the roughly 1,069,970 acres, so any future mining development there ends. The cost is bounded: valid existing mining rights are grandfathered in and later-acquired lands are withdrawn only going forward. Federal agencies would also bear the cost of writing a management plan within two years, reviewing it annually, and funding tribal cooperative agreements and grants.

drawbacks.text: The withdrawal permanently forecloses new mineral development — including uranium — across the monument area, which a supporter of domestic mineral production would object to on the grounds that it shrinks the domestic supply of uranium and other minerals on federal land.

Locations of cultural resources at the monument would be exempt from Freedom of Information Act disclosure, and the Tribal commission would be exempt from the Federal Advisory Committee Act, both of which reduce public transparency about how the land is managed.

The bill layers new federal obligations onto the land — a comprehensive management plan due within two years, annual plan reviews, grants and cooperative agreements with tribes — an ongoing administrative and budgetary commitment for the agencies and taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and durable: permanent watershed protection for the Grand Canyon ecosystem, formal tribal co-stewardship of an ancestral homeland, and locked-in recreational access that local economies depend on. The costs are narrow and largely prospective — mining companies lose future claims they do not currently hold, and agencies take on planning work. The transparency exemptions (FOIA carve-out for cultural sites, FACA exemption for the tribal commission) are real but standard for protecting sensitive archaeological sites. On balance the bill was designed to change very little for current users while ending new mining development, which is exactly the tradeoff its opponents would have contested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, without a hearing, markup, or floor vote, until the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on July 12, 2023, together with Representative Ruben Gallego, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day.

The bill would have designated a 1,069,970-acre Grand Canyon national monument, withdrawn the land from new mining claims and mineral and geothermal leasing subject to valid existing rights, and created a Tribal commission of 12 Associated Tribes to guide management.
It preserved existing uses in detail — hunting and fishing under state law, grazing established before enactment, water rights and compacts, utility corridors, and general public access.
That referral was the last action ever taken: no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote followed, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: On the substance, the tribes and the public came out largely ahead anyway: President Biden designated the same Baaj Nwaavjo I'tah Kukveni Grand Canyon National Monument by proclamation in August 2023, delivering the land protection without Congress. For the bill itself, the mining industry and the House committee majority were spared a vote, while its sponsors gained a legislative record to point to.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tribes and public, via Biden's proclamation instead

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured its referral to the Natural Resources Committee, which he served on as ranking Democrat.

for.name: Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Joined Grijalva in introducing the bill on the day it was filed.

for.name: President Joe Biden
for.what_they_did: Designated the Baaj Nwaavjo I'tah Kukveni Grand Canyon National Monument by proclamation in August 2023, accomplishing the bill's core purpose through executive authority rather than legislation.

for.name: Associated Grand Canyon Tribes coalition
for.role: Coalition of 12 tribes including the Havasupai, Hopi, Hualapai, Navajo Nation, and Zuni
for.what_they_did: Advocated for the national monument and the tribal co-stewardship provisions the bill codified.

against.name: Bruce Westerman
against.what_they_did: The Republican-led committee took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting it expire.

against.name: Uranium and hardrock mining industry
against.role: Mining claim holders and exploration companies near the Grand Canyon
against.what_they_did: Opposed the monument designation and the permanent withdrawal of the area from new mining claims.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the split was never tested; in the record, every sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Natural Resources Committee, which could have moved the bill, never acted.

industries.note: The bill would withdraw about 1,069,970 acres from new mining claims and from mineral and geothermal leasing, ending future mine development near the canyon while grandfathering valid existing rights. The industry's gain — opening new ground near the Grand Canyon — comes at the expense of the watershed and recreation economy the public uses.

The bill explicitly guarantees continued hunting, fishing, camping, hiking, and mountain biking, and its findings call recreation the primary driver of sustainable economic development in nearby communities. Monument status also protects the scenery and watershed those businesses depend on.
Grazing established or permitted before enactment would continue unchanged under all applicable laws, locking in existing ranchers' access while excluding no one new.
